accuracy.evidence: Every quotation was checked against the Folger text of Macbeth: 'Stars, hide your fires...' (1.4, spoken just after Duncan names Malcolm Prince of Cumberland), 'Look like th' innocent flower, / But be the serpent under't' and 'unsex me here' (1.5), the Porter's 'equivocator' (2.3), 'dark night strangles the travelling lamp', the falcon killed by 'a mousing owl' and Duncan's horses that 'eat each other' (2.4), the show of eight kings (4.1), 'brave Macbeth' (1.2) and 'this dead butcher' (final scene). Context facts match the British Library and Britannica: first staged about 1606, James I's Daemonologie (1597), James's claimed descent from Banquo, Henry Garnet's 1606 trial and defence of equivocation, the divine right of kings and the Great Chain of Being. Wherefore = why and thou as the familiar or lower-status 'you' follow the OED glosses.

misconceptions.evidence: Targets the documented GCSE slips named in examiner reports and Bitesize guidance: wherefore read as where (first prediction, a distractor tile 'where', p1, challenge), literal paraphrase of imagery (step 2 feedback, 'Hide a real snake' and 'a real dagger' options), reading only half a line, treating regicide as a crime against one man (prediction, challenge), bolted-on biography as context (step 5 message, p5, sorter visual), and claiming character change without start-and-end evidence (m7).

lab_distinct.evidence: The mechanics are specific to reading Shakespeare in context: an old-word decoder with a deliberate 'where' trap, a line-by-line paraphrase cycler for one named speech, a drag-to-swap Great Chain of Being, a hunt for disorder signs in Act 2 Scene 4, and links from play details to 1606 events. None of this transfers to another topic by changing labels; it shares no mechanism with the evidence or critical-lens labs.

lab_teaches.evidence: The learner discovers each idea by doing it: the wrong tile explains why wherefore is not where, each wrong paraphrase names whether it is too literal or reverses the meaning, swapping the chain explains why the king must sit above nobles, the disorder hunt shows nature reacting to the broken chain, and the context links only accept the fact that explains the detail. Completion messages then state the rule.

predictions.evidence: Four predictions, each with a tempting wrong answer that the next task disproves: 'Where are you, Romeo?', hiding 'the stars', the people choosing the king by vote, and regicide as a crime against one man.

challenge_feedback.evidence: Seven items rotate the answer position. Each wrong option carries a tag with its own message: the wherefore/where slip, too-literal reading, reading half a line, thinking too small about regicide, bolted-on context, a false claim about 1606, and an old-word misread. The answer is shown after a miss, and the canvas keeps a decoder and the chain on screen.

readability.evidence: Learner text scores about grade 2.4 and adult text about 7.4 on the repo's Flesch-Kincaid check (limits 6.5 and 9.5). Sentences are short, every old word is glossed when first used, and quotations are kept to a line or two.

no_filler.evidence: Each paragraph teaches a skill (decoding, paraphrase, context) or a fact the lab uses. The adult text lists concrete mistakes and one home activity. Lab copy is instructions and feedback only, and no gate filler phrase matches.

mobile.evidence: Checked on iPhone 13 screenshots: two columns of large tiles for the decoder and context links (12 px wrapped text for the longer facts), full-width paraphrase cards with three lines of room each, six full-width chain cards and disorder rows, and buttons of at least 44 px under the canvas. Nothing is clipped; the chain header hint is hidden on narrow screens to avoid overlap.

accessibility.evidence: Every gesture has a button twin: pick-word then '= meaning' buttons, 'Change line N', '↑ rank' moves, 'Mark N' and 'Detail N' / 'Fact A' links with full text in aria-labels. The canvas aria-label reports links made, the current paraphrase, the chain order or the marked events after each action. axe (WCAG 2.1 AA) is clean in both themes on desktop and iPhone.
